# Executive summary 

Global demand for copper has been severely impacted by the downturn in manufacturing activity and destocking.  After growing by a modest 2.7% to 17.9Mt in 2007, global copper consumption contracted by 0.5% in 2008 to just below 17.9Mt.  However, this year we are forecasting that consumption will decline by 2.8% to ~17.4Mt.  The bulk of the contraction is forecast to occur in the world’s mature economies where consumption is forecast to fall by 7.4% to ~7Mt. 

During the current price cycle, which is projected to run from 2002 to 2009, we forecast that global consumption will grow at an average rate of 2% p.a.  Largely responsible for the lower growth is contracting demand in Western Europe, North America and Japan, which reflects the mature state of the economies and the relocation of copper semi plants to other regions where labour costs and energy costs are much lower. 

We forecast that base case mine production capability will increase by 3.5% this year to ~16.2Mt. Between 2002 and 2009 the average annual growth rate in base case world copper mine production capability (excluding highly probable and probable projects) is forecast to be 2.1% p.a., including 1.7% p.a. ex-concentrates and 3.5% p.a from SxEw sources. 

Base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 1% p.a. between 2009 (inclusive) and 2020 with mine output falling from a peak of ~17.9Mt in 2012 to ~13.8Mt in 2020.  At the same time, demand for additional mine production to meet increased market requirements for refined metal will create an implied shortfall in mine output of ~0.6Mt/a in 2014, 4.4Mt/a in 2017 and 7.4Mt/a by 2020. 

We now expect base case global copper smelter production capability to reach 14.2Mt/a in 2009 (-1%), before rising to ~16.1Mt in 2010 (+13.5%) and 17.5Mt in 2011 (+8.5%).  During the current price cycle (2002-2009) base case global smelter production capability is forecast to rise at a rate of 2% p.a. before rising to 2.3% p.a. during the period 2009-2020. 

We forecast a global market surplus of ~600kt for the year.  This is little changed for our previous surplus estimate of 590kt and stocks, at 65 days of consumption, have returned to more normal levels. Nevertheless, we have raised our average price forecast for the year, lifting it from $4186/t ($1.90/lb) previously to $4935/t.  The 18% gain in price reflects a much stronger than anticipated price environment for the year so far, especially during Q3, brought about by much healthier than expected Chinese demand.

# Demand analysis 

## Overview 

**Global economy beginning to stabilise** After a dismal twelve months, the global economy is finally beginning to show some stability and many of the world’s major economies appear to be poised to begin what is likely to be a long road to recovery.  As far as copper is concerned, with the notable exceptions of India and China, consumption has contracted in all of the world’s major economies with the combination of plunging end user demand and de-stocking at all levels of the global supply chain resulting in double-digit declines in most of the world’s mature economies. 

**Mature economy copper demand forecast to decline for the third consecutive year** Refined copper consumption in the world’s mature economies will decline for the third consecutive year in 2009.  After contracting by 4% in 2007 and 7.4% in 2008, consumption is forecast to fall by a further 14.3% in 2009 to 5.9Mt, its lowest level since 1983.  Given the depth of the downturn, the recovery in copper consumption will be slow and we are unlikely to see mature economy copper consumption recover to the 7.8Mt/a average seen between 2000 and 2008 at any point during the forecast period.  In 2010, the combined impact of the various stimulus packages deployed by the governments of the mature economies will result in copper consumption within the mature economies growing by 1.3%.  In 2011 mature economy copper demand growth is forecast to grow more strongly, increasing by 3.1% to 6.2Mt.  This will reflect the combination of pent up consumer and business demand, re-stocking and the coming to fruition of many government-backed infrastructure initiatives.  Thereafter, copper demand growth will be curbed by the negative impact of the stimulus measures, such as higher taxes, lower consumer and business spending, cuts to public services and investment. Demand within the mature economies will also be hampered by increased market share of global demand from some of the developing economies, namely China and India.  As a consequence we forecast that copper consumption will decline by 1.7 p.a. over the period 2012 to 2020 to 5.3Mt in 2020. 

**Healthy growth forecast in copper demand in the developing economies** In the developing economies we forecast that demand will grow by 4.4% this year to 11.4Mt.  This will follow growth of 8.1% in 2007 and 4.5% in 2008 to 10.5Mt and 10.9Mt respectively.  Supporting the healthy gain for this year is a 20% increase in Chinese refined copper consumption to just over 6Mt.  This reflects China’s stimulus package, major increases in credit availability and ongoing investment within the power sector.  In 2010 we project that investment within the power sector will be maintained, helping Chinese refined copper consumption to increase by a further 7% to ~6.4Mt.  This will lift developing demand growth by 5.3% to 12Mt while in 2011 stronger growt

h of 7.7% is forecast with demand in the developing economies reaching just under 13Mt.  The rise will reflect restocking, pent-up consumer and business demand and the full effects of the various infrastructure-related stimulus measures.  These factors will also help to support demand growth within the mature economies.  Thus we forecast that global refined copper consumption will grow by 6.2% in 2011 to 19.1Mt, up from 3.9% in 2020, to ~18mt and -2.8% in 2009 to ~17.4Mt.  For the forecast period as a whole (2009-2020) we estimate that global demand for copper will increase by 2.9% p.a., reaching 25.2Mt by 2020.

**Demand forecast to grow by 2% p.a. during the current price cycle** During the current price cycle, which is projected to run from 2002 to 2009, we forecast that global consumption will grow at an average rate of 2% p.a. (see table below) which is below the average annual growth rate in the previous price cycle which ran between 1993 and 2002.  Largely responsible for the lower growth is contracting demand in Western Europe, North America and Japan, which reflects the mature state of the economies and the relocation of copper semi plants to other regions where labour costs and energy costs are much lower.  Increased imports of copper and copper alloy products from China will also be responsible for the falling demand growth.  Nevertheless, strong growth in the Eastern Bloc is anticipated.  This is particularly true of Russia and China where demand is forecast to rise at an average rate of 13.2% p.a. and 7.2% p.a. respectively.  In Russia strong growth in the domestic production of copper wire rod will be largely responsible for this increase while in China it will be robust growth in the domestic output of both wire rod and copper semi products.

lapse in demand for many Chinese made goods in the world’s mature economies. The economy was initially hit hard by the collapse of export markets in the final months of last year and, although they have show some signs of improvement recently, both China’s imports and exports remain at depressed levels. ##### **Chinese trade** 50.00%

**Chinese benefit from quick response to the global economic downturn** The reason that the Chinese economy has shown such resilience despite the collapse in foreign trade is the rapid response of the Chinese government to the crisis in October 2008 when it unveiled a $586Bn stimulus package. In addition to the package the authorities also eased restrictions on the availability of credit, a policy that had been in force for the past couple of years. The authorities set a target of $730Bn for new bank loans in 2009. However, during the first seven months of the year new lending by the country’s banks soared to $1.1Tn. **Chinese capital spending up sharply this year** As a consequence of these developments capital spending has risen sharply this year, helping to offset the downturn in the export-led manufacturing sector. Urban fixed asset investment has also grown strongly, increasing by 33% year on year in August, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS). This level has been sustained since May and is well above the 26.5% annual gain recorded in February. The country’s central and western provinces have particularly benefited from ongoing infrastructure investment. **Chinese consumer spending stimulated** In addition to boosting spending on capital assets, such as large scale infrastructure projects around the country, both state and regional governments have tried to stimulate consumer spending. This has been dampened by economic uncertainty and rising unemployment. Government policies have ranged from tax breaks to spending vouchers on a variety of discretionary spending items ranging from homes through to cars, white goods and even tourist attractions. The most successful of these programmes has been in the auto sector where tax breaks on sales of small cars have led to a surge in sales throughout China, especially in the country’s rural areas. According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers, car sales in the first eight months of the year totalled 8.3M u

nits, a year-on-year rise of 29.2%.  Production, meanwhile, climbed by 26.6% to 8.3M units.  The increase in domestic car sales outstripped the decline in exports which fell by 60% year-on-year during the same eight month period to 186kt. 

**Spending vouchers on white goods support copper demand** Meanwhile the success of the spending vouchers on white goods was noticeable in the latest data from the National Bureau of Statistics which showed the production of refrigerators, freezers and computers rising annually by 15%, 12.2% and 15.9% respectively during the first eight months of the year.  Nevertheless, China’s strong growth in copper consumption so far this year has mainly been supported by strong orders from the power sector.  This was apparent from the operating rates at key wire and cable plants during July which reached 71.8%, up from 71.1% in June.  These rates are expected to be maintained during Q3 while increasing slightly in Q4 as China continues to invest within the power sector.  Investment within this sector is reported to reach 580Bn Yuan ($85Bn) this year. 

**New capacity within copper semis sector due to come on stream** In addition, the copper market has also been supported by the ongoing development of China’s copper semis sector.  One of the largest projects includes Chinalco Luoyang Copper’s new 100kt/a high-precision electronic copper strip and plate plant.  The company recently reported that production, which is expected to begin in September this year, will reach 30kt this year before rising to full capacity in 2010.  Elsewhere, Zhejiang Hailiang reported that it hopes to raise its copper alloy pipe production capacity to 260kt/a this year, up from 160kt/a currently.  The increased capacity reflects the forthcoming completion of new production lines in both China and Vietnam.  Capacity at its three copper alloy plants in Zhejiang will increase by 30kt/a by the end of this year while production at its Vietnam plant will increase by 70kt/a by year end.  Finally, the  Jinchuan Group reported this month that it expects to complete a new 60kt/a copper-nickel alloy pipe, rod and extrusion plant by the end of this year. The new 60kt/a capacity will be split as follows: 32.5kt for copper alloy rods and wire rods, 15.8kt white copper pipes, 10.7kt brass and purple pipes and 1kt extrusion products.  The output will be used in shipbuilding, desalination, galvanizing, electrical appliances, automobile and military applications.  The new capacity being brought on line will not only help to boost Chinese demand for copper in this year but in 2010 as well.  Taking all of the above into account we forecast that Chinese demand for copper will grow by 20% this year, to 6Mt, before increasing by a further 7% in 2010 to ~6.4Mt.

1 and 6% in 2012 to 7Mt and 7.4Mt respectively. Between 2009 and 2020, Chinese consumption growth is forecast to average 7.3% p.a. This will lead to an increase in consumption of ~0.6Mt/a, raising consumption to ~11.6Mt by 2020. ## USA **USA showing signs of emerging from the recession** Just as North America was at the forefront of the plunge into recession, it is also showing signs of being amongst the first to emerge from recession. The maximum impact of the Obama administration’s stimulus package has been felt this summer and the pick-up in US manufacturing capacity and the positive impact that this has had on its northern neighbour, Canada, should see economic momentum build during the coming months. As of August US industrial production has posted two consecutive months of month-on-month growth, the first time that this has occurred since November and December of 2007. However, 7M jobs have been lost since the beginning of the recession and according to the US labour department in August, 26.3M workers were underutilised of which 14.9M were unemployed. The unemployment rate of 9.7% was its highest since 1983. This pool of unemployed and underemployed workers will act as a drag on consumer spending and the housing markets and, as a consequence, the US recovery will likely be tempered for much of next year and it will not be until 2011 that growth gets fully underway **IP data highlights the extent of the downturn in US manufacturing** An indication of the extent of the collapse in US manufacturing comes from the latest estimates of industrial production and capacity utilisation published by the Federal Reserve which show that utilisation rates in the manufacturing sector in August were just 66.6%, well below the 19722008 average rate of 79.6% and lower than that seen in the recessions of the 1970s and early 1980s. Based on the response following previous US recessions, and even when helped by the permanent elimination of unwanted/obsolete capacity, utilisation rates are likely to take 2-5 years to recover to pre-recession levels. **US housing market stabilising** The recession began with the housing market which, after falling since 2006, seems to be stabilising, with the number of housing starts creeping towards the upper end of the 500-600k unit range seen this year. Although

this rate is extremely low, it is allowing for the drawdown of excessive inventories of new homes built during the bubble.  However, demand for new homes is likely to be hit around the end of the year as the number of foreclosures builds.  It is unlikely that there will be a dramatic acceleration in the pace of construction of new homes until inventories are drawn down, a process which will probably take two to three years to complete, which suggests that demand growth for copper from this sector will be restrained at best.  Whereas the residential construction sector is showing some signs of stability, the non-residential construction sector will decline well into next year.  The US National Association of Realtors is forecasting that annual rents for office, industrial and retail properties are forecast to decline by 6-14% this year and by 5-12% next year.  Declining rents and increasing vacancy rates are likely to slow the construction of new properties for much of 2010.  Further evidence of the likely weakness in the US non-residential construction sector comes from the American Institute of Architects’ billing index which reached 43.1 in July.  While this was five

The weakness of the index suggests that non-residential construction sector will remain depressed well into 2010.  This weakness will undermine any strength in demand for copper wire and cable and copper plumbing and air conditioning tube. 

**Automotive sector still a drag on the US economy** The other drag on the US economy will continue to be the automotive sector, which despite the boost from the cash for clunkers programme will emerge from the recession a shadow of its former self.  While the ‘cash for clunkers’ programme lifted US car sales by 16% in year on year terms in August and total light vehicle sales by 1%, it has not been enough to make a major difference to the year to date figures which remain appalling.  Total light vehicle sales in the first eight months of the year fell annually by 28% to 7M units. The situation is even worse in terms of production, with output of cars and light trucks through to August totalling just 3.3M units, down 47% year on year.  However, on a brighter note, the success of the programme has significantly depleted automotive inventories at all levels from the showroom back to the manufacturing plants, and the replenishment of stocks will provide a much needed fillip to copper consumption in the form of copper wire and cable.  The success of the programme has prompted automotive consultants JD Power to increase its 2009 sales forecast to 10.3M units, up from 10M units previously.  However, while the programme may have attracted consumers back into America’s car show rooms there is a danger that the bo

ost to sales will have come at the expense of sales that might have otherwise occurred later this year and in 2010.  As a result JD Power has dropped its 2010 sales forecast from 11.6M units to 11.5M units, or 32% lower than the 2000-2007 US annual sales average of 16.8M units. 

**Consumers will be offered rebates on certain home appliances** The popularity of the ‘cash for clunkers’ scheme may be repeated with a modest new scheme designed to stimulate the purchase of energy efficient home appliances. The US Department of Energy (DoE) is making nearly $300 million in stimulus funding available for states to offer consumers rebates on certain home appliances.  The states must submit their plans specifying appliance energy categories and products covered by the scheme to the DoE by October 15, with the scheme scheduled to end on November 30.  However, the scheme is unlikely to have a significant impact on the US home appliance market which, according to the US Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers, saw shipments totalling 68.2M units in 2008, a year on year decline of 8.9%.  Whirlpool, the world’s largest producer of home appliances reported that its North American sales (excluding currency effects) fell by 14% to $2.4Bn in the second quarter of the year.  Based on current market conditions the company said that it expects its US shipments in 2009 to decline by 10-12% in year on year terms. 

**US copper demand remains very poor** Despite the slightly encouraging outlook for copper, demand remains extremely poor.  Production of copper wire rod and shipments of copper and copper alloy products continued to record double digit declines.  The American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS) reported that the production of copper wire rod declined by 25.4% (-205kt) during the first six months of the year from the corresponding period in 2008.  Meanwhile the association reported that the shipments of copper and copper alloy products dropped annually by 32.1% (-210kt) during the same eight months period.  Unsurprisingly those products consumed within the construction sector recorded the largest declines with the production of copper tube and copper plate sheet and strip falling by 25% and 37.5% respectively during Jan-Aug from a year earlier. 

**US demand for copper forecast to fall by ~11% in 2009** Although we expect that the rate of decline in US demand for copper will slow during H2, we forecast that US refined copper consumption will decline by 10.9% overall this year to ~1.7Mt.  A small recovery is expected in 2010, with demand increasing by 0.8% to ~1.8Mt.  However, in 2011 US refined copper consumption is forecast to increase by a much stronger 3.9%, to just over 1.8Mt, as consumer and business confidence improves and demand from the construction sector picks up. 

**Negative growth forecast for US copper demand during 2009-2020** Over the forecast period 2009-2020 we project that US demand for copper will decline by 1.8% p.a., reflecting struc

tural changes in the global economy which will see manufacturing and semis capacity relocating to lower wage economies, such as Mexico and China. There will also be an increase in the amount of demand satisfied by imports rather than domestic production. By 2020 we forecast that North American consumption will total just under 1.6Mt. This will account for ~6.3% of the global total compared with 11% in 2008. ## Europe **Germany and France emerge from recession** As has been the case elsewhere in the world, government stimulus measures and monetary easing by the European and other central banks in the region have pulled the worst of the sting from the recession, thereby allowing Europe’s major economies of France and Germany to emerge from recession. This is well clear of the 31.96 level plumbed in January and suggests that the contraction of the German manufacturing sector is coming to a halt. However, the same cannot be said for the German construction sector, with its PMI suggesting that it is still contracting, albeit at a more moderate pace. ##### **German manufacturing and services recover, but construction is still struggling** 70

As has happened elsewhere in the world, Germany’s automotive sector has benefited from a scrapping scheme which has boosted car sales. The programme has been highly successful, boosting German car and light vehicle sales during the first eight months of the year by 26% year on year to 2.8M units. However, rather than boosting production the rise in sales has drawn down inventories with production over

the same period falling by 24% year on year to 3.1M units. However, the scrapping scheme ran out of funds and was terminated at the end of August.  With the German authorities ruling out an extension, sales are likely to plunge in the coming months and will remain depressed throughout next year. 

**Car schemes introduced to boost sales** Other major European countries have also introduced various schemes designed to boost car sales.  However, the boost will similarly be temporary and sales will fall away after the traditional August drop off.  Meanwhile, car production in Western Europe has continued to fall.  Output during the first eight months of the year totalled 6.9M units, representing a year-on-year decline of 25%.  Automotive consultants JD Power is forecasting a 10% contraction in the Western European car markets in 2010, led by a 29% fall in Germany. 

**Aurubis report improving market conditions** The small improvement in European economic activity was reiterated by Aurubis, the region’s largest producer of copper wire rod and shapes, who reported a small improvement in demand for its copper products during Q2.  It announced that the low point in its wire rod market point was reached in April, with state economic stimulus packages helping to lift demand for automotive wiring.  Meanwhile the company’s order intake for copper cast shapes stabilised in May before recovering in June.  Although the recovery in demand for the company’s copper wire rod and copper products has been sluggish so far, Aurubis expects the upturn to strengthen in the coming months.  This is encouraging in light of the sharp downturn experienced during Q2, when the company’s production of copper wire rod and copper cast shapes declined by 37% (-87kt) and 55% (-36kt) respectively from a year earlier. 

**Italian copper demand very weak** Elsewhere in Italy demand remained extremely weak during Q2, reflecting overinvestment in the construction sector and the subsequent over-supply in housing stock.  This was highlighted by Assomet, Italy’s nonferrous organisation, reporting a 30.3% year on year decline in copper and copper alloy products output during Q2.  For H1 as a whole, the organisation reported a 29.5% year-on-year decline in production. 

**European copper demand not expected to recover fully until 2011** For Western Europe as a whole we forecast that after contracting by 6.8% in 2008, European copper consumption will contract by a further 11.7% this year to ~3Mt. While demand is expected to stabilise in 2010, with growth of 1.4%, a full recovery in demand is not expected until 2011 where consumption is forecast to increase by 3% to ~3.1Mt.  The healthy gain will reflect both re-stocking and pent-up consumer and business demand.  By 2012 the global economy will return to normal and increased investment should result in the residential and non-residential construction sectors recovering which will help consumption growth stay positive, albeit moderately.  We fo

recast growth of 0.9% in 2012 and 1.1% in 2013 to ~3.2Mt. Thereafter, copper consumption growth is forecast to decrease on an annual basis, falling to 2.6mt in 2020. Likewise with the US, the contraction reflects increased cheaper imports from developing economies in Asia, including China, as well from Eastern Europe where labour and energy costs are much cheaper. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - September 2009 Page 10 of 70 Long Term Outlook - Copper ## Japan **Japanese economy recovering** A strong rise in Japanese industrial production during Q2 provided further evidence that the economy continued to recover. According to Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI), industrial production (IP) increased by 8.3% in Q2 from Q1. This represented the first rise in five months and was the sharpest quarter-on-quarter gain ever recorded. The increase reflected government stimulus measures as well as rising exports to China. A ¥25Tr ($265Bn) economic stimulus plan has helped to boost sales of autos and consumer electronics. Meanwhile rising exports to China have prompted increased spending on infrastructure projects. However, despite the positive increase in industrial activity production still remains weak. According to METI, if IP increases by its projected growth, production will still only be 80% of the level achieved during last autumn. Even if IP grew by 5% each quarter, METI forecasts that it will still take a year to reach the production levels achieved during the latter months of 2008. Indeed it is unlikely that domestic demand will be lifted by capital investment and wage increases any time soon as companies suffer from excess production capacity and manpower. **Small improvement in shipments of copper wire and cable** As with the economy, shipments of copper wire and cable continued to recover, albeit very moderately. According to the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association, shipments rose by 8.9% in July from June. However, on an annual basis shipments declined by 20.5% from July last year. Nevertheless this was still encouraging because this represented the smallest drop on an annual basis since December last year, suggesting that the pace of the downturn is slowing. Data from the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association showed that demand for wire and cable has improved since May, when shipments fell by 31% year on year to their lowest level since February

1975. Anecdotal evidence suggests that the improvement largely reflected rising demand from the auto and semiconductor sectors. Latest government data show that the production of autos fell by 33% year on year in June. This compared with a 41% decline in May and a 47% in April from a year earlier. However, in July auto sales fell by only 3% from a year earlier which is encouraging because the large discrepancy between sales and production will lead to re-stocking and, in return, rising orders for copper automotive wire and cable. **Demand from the construction sector remains weak** Elsewhere within the wire and cable markets demand remained weak, especially within the construction sector. The Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association reported a 22.1% annual decline in wire and cable shipments to the construction sector during July. According to the Association this mainly reflected a prolonged dip in corporate spending and housing starts. Japanese housing starts fell by 25.8% during the first five months of the year from the corresponding period in 2008. Unfortunately no overall recovery in the wire and cable sector will occur until a sustainable pick-up in orders from the construction takes place. This is because shipments of wire and cable to the construction sector account for ~40% of total wire and cable shipments. With this in mind we continue to forecast a 28.9% decline in Japanese refined copper consumption this year to ~850kt. ## Changes to smelter production forecasts since Q2 **We have lowered our near-term global smelter production capability estimates** The changes made to our forecast global smelter output since the last long term outlook report are also shown in the main report. The lower figure for this year partly reflects the knock-on effect of industrial action at some mine sites that is leading to shortage of concentrate feed at some smelters. This is particularly true of the Vale Inco strike that has led to Xstrata’s Kidd Creek smelter running short of concentrate feed. Vale Inco supplies +/-50kt/a of copper-in-concentrates to Kidd Creek (as well as 70kt/a of anodes to the CCR refinery in Montreal) and the combination of the extended maintenance shutdown in Sudbury plus the ongoing strike has severely limited feed to the Xstrata smelter. The growth in China’s primary copper smelting capacity in recent years has occurred at a time when there have been substantial disruptions to copper-in-concentrate output. New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply. A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles. New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it. Old scrap is generated fr

om worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply 

## Scrapping rates 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often lea

ding to plant closures, particularly in the USA. This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining). #### **GDP Forecast Changes** 

Thanks to significant fiscal spending, ultra loose monetary policy and some co-ordination between the G-20, recovery is now underway in the major developed economies.  After unprecedented periods of consecutive contraction in the major advanced economies, the recession is technically over.  The authorities have been largely successful in managing to limit the effects of the financial crisis, supporting both corporates and households through the worst using an array of ever more imaginative tools.  Notably, key money markets have normalised and the US housing market appears to have bottomed out - the necessary conditions for recovery to start.  Looking ahead, the global economy has around 6- 9 months to get back on its feet before the pain relief provided by countercyclical fiscal and monetary policy starts to fade. Fiscal stimulus cannot (and will not) last into the second half of 2010 and the monetary tightening cycle must begin within the next 18 months to prevent another bubble induced crash within the next 5 years or so. 

Under ‘normal’ circumstances, economies tend to recover from recession in a fairly predictable fashion.  Monetary policy is loosened into the downswing and automatic stabilisers (such as unemployment benefit and a lower tax burden) kick in to limit the contraction.  With time, a floor is reached and the economy moves into recovery.  Households start to consume more as real disposable income rises and corporates resume investment projects as confidence returns.  Such a V-shaped recovery is characterised by a period of sub-trend growth (the recession) followed by a period of above trend growth (the recovery), helping to bring the economy back to where it would have been if the recession had not taken place. 

This recession is different.  It is synchronised – globally – and has been preceded by a financial crisis.  Both of these factors make it particularly severe.  In most of the developed world, recovery will be weak and drawn out as households struggle to rebuild their balance sheets and household consumption remains subdued.  Bankruptcies will continue through 2009.  Unemployment will continue to rise through H1 2010.  Coupled with a banking system still reeling from write-downs, recovery is set to be jobless and creditless in most of the major developed economies. 

The story is different for the major developing economies.  Through the use of effective monetary policy and direct interventionist fiscal policy, some economies have managed to avoid the effects of the severe collapse in global trade with enviable success (to date).  As in our March forecast, the non-OECD is set to avoid contraction altogether in 2009, with growth forecast to rebound in 2010 to 5.4% (compared with 3.7% forecast in March).

#### **United States of America** 

After a record four consecutive quarters of contraction, US GDP appears to have stabilised.  We forecast growth of 2% (quarter on quarter annualised) in Q3 and 3% in Q4.  On an annual basis, we expect GDP to contract 2.8% in 2009 and to grow by 2.0% in 2010 and 2011. 

Four factors lie behind the upward revision to our US GDP growth forecast for 2009 and 2010.

Although backward looking, these revisions are important because they change the position of the US economy in the recession cycle: the US now appears to be further through the recession than had been previously reported and this has implications for the timing and shape of the expected recovery. 

Inventory cycle boost: at the beginning of a recession – a time of extreme uncertainty – it is typical for firms to cut back on production and draw down inventories to fulfil orders until the production outlook improves.  Through Q2, stock drawdown has accelerated and we now believe firms are close to their desired level of stock.  This marks the turning point for production and based on this inventory cycle, industrial production looks set to rebound in the second half of 2009.  With only a transitory impact on growth – lasting two to three quarters on average, we expect this inventory boost to dissipate markedly in the first quarter of 2010.

##### **Why the lacklustre outlook for 2010?** In order of significance, US economic growth in a recovery period is driven by: household consumption; inventories; government spending; and business investment. Analysis of past US recoveries shows that approximately 50% of growth in the first year of a recovery is due to consumption, rising to 60% in the second year of recovery. Inventories are the next most important contributor but the positive effect is only enjoyed in the first year of recovery because this effect is transitory. Business investment takes over as the second most important driver of growth in the second year of expansion as corporates start to invest after holding off over the uncertain recessionary period. With consumption accounting for 70% of domestic demand in the US and with the consumer the key driver of growth in a recovery phase, the outlook for the US consumer is critical to the overall macroeconomic outlook. The US consumer will determine the speed and magnitude of the US recovery through 2010 and 2011. As households try to protect themselves from negative shocks such as unemployment or lower wages/ hours worked, savings rates typically rise through a recession. With savings rates rising (in most major economies), household consumption can only be driven by growth in real disposable income. We forecast a lacklustre 2010 recovery because the drivers of real disposable income growth are missing or have already been enjoyed with little effect on consumption. In summary, the five drivers of income growth in a recovery phase are as follows: Private sector wage growth: private sector wage growth is highly correlated with growth in hours worked. In August 2009, the average number of hours worked in the US was close to a record low (33 hrs per week). Starting from such a low base, it is u

nlikely that private sector wage growth will drive income growth through H2 2009 and into 2010. 

Government transfers: public sector wages and direct non-work related transfers (such as unemployment insurance benefits) often support household income in the recovery phase.  Non fiscal stimulus support will fade through 2010 with state and local governments actually reducing spending and employment in an effort to control growing deficits. 

Lower inflation/ deflation: lower price growth/ lower prices (in July, the PCE deflator and CPI were both negative) increases the purchasing power of households.  Given that prices are unlikely to fall much more (month-on-month) much of this stimulus has already been enjoyed. 

Tax relief: some of the fiscal stimulus package will go to support households earning less than $200,000 but further tax relief through 2010 looks unlikely given the rising federal fiscal deficit.  In 2011, overall tax relief is likely to be reversed as the Bush tax cuts expire. 

Household wealth appreciation: with equity markets rising around the world, household equity portfolios and pensions will have risen over the past 6 months.  However, overall household wealth has fallen so much over the past year or so that the majority of the recent gains will only act to recoup some of those losses.

After a severe contraction we now output bottomed out in Q1 and have made upward revisions to growth for 2009 and 2010. Germany is now expected to contract by 4.9% in 2009 (from 5.3% forecast in June)

and to grow by an anaemic 1.0% in 2010.  In the short-term, quarter-on-quarter growth is forecast to remain positive in H2 2009, at 0.8% in Q3 and 0.3% in Q4. 

Some of the upward revision is due to a base effect, with the German authorities making downward revisions to 2008 GDP growth – from 1.3% to 1.0%.  However, the majority of the revision has been driven by a stronger than expected consumer, further inventory cycle support and stabilisation in the export market. 

Consumption: to date, the German consumer has remained resilient, with household consumption falling less than in other parts of the developed world.  The German consumer has been protected by limited unemployment growth, rising disposable income (thanks to generous wage deals struck in 2008), low inflation, greater welfare benefits, tax cuts and a €5bn car scrappage scheme.  On a structural basis, the German household has also been less reliant on credit to fuel spending, has a more robust balance sheet and has not experienced the adverse shock to wealth resulting from bursting asset bubbles as in other major economies.  We expect the German consumer to become less resilient through H2 2009 and into 2010 as unemployment starts to rise (more aggressively). 

Net trade: trade has been the conduit through which the global recession has affected Germany most.  With exports collapsing at the end of 2008 and imports remaining relatively strong (buoyed by sustained consumer demand), net trade has driven the contraction in German output.  Clearly, the outlook for net trade is critical to the GDP forecast.  Over the past quarter, the collapse in exports appears to have stabilised.  However, looking forward we do not expect a significant rebound in trade as global export volumes are expected to contract by approximately 10% this year and are only forecast to recover slowly through 2010. 

Investment: While there are encouraging signs of a slowing in the pace of investment contraction (gross fixed capital formation actually increased by 0.8% in Q2 2009 and investment in construction reached 1.4%), German business investment is likely to fall by over 10% year-on-year in 2009.  This fall has been driven by a lack of credit availability and concerns about excess capacity.  With ongoing problems in the banking sector (limiting access to finance) and only a moderate outlook for exports (which is having a knock on effect for expectations), investment is unlikely to bounce back significantly in 2010. 

Government: the German Government has enacted several policies to help stabilise the economy and provide support to the ailing banking sector.  Specifically, the authorities were the first to implement a successful _Cash for Clunkers_ program – which has helped support industrial production, and have recently agreed to cover part of the labour cost facing firms if they agree hold on to workers. South Africa has now reported 4 consecutive quarters of contraction (2.8% Q2 2009) and appears to be lagging the majority of the developing world out of recession.  The South African economy has been adversely affected by: (i) lower commodity prices which, coupled with a sharp contraction in mining output, have led to a sharp fall mining contribution to output growth; (ii) tough financing conditions/ credit availability – tightening household spending and making private investment more difficult/ costly; and (iii) low business confidence as the downturn in global demand affects the export position and households shy away from spending.

#### **Germany** 

Germany implemented one of the most generous _Cash for Clunkers_ incentive schemes in Europe, offering €2,500 in trade-in discounts.  Following its introduction in February this year, the government extended its total budget on the scheme to €5bn (US$7.1bn) in March in an attempt to keep it in place until the end of 2009.  As a result, new-car registrations in Germany have soared.  In August, they rose 28% year-on-year. 

Nearly two million German consumers participated in the program, which largely benefited mass-market auto makers like Volkswagen AG and Ford.  But sceptics say the program simply delayed a slump.  But this boost in demand for car manufacturers was limited to domestic sales.  German car companies exported only 1.2 Mn new cars from January to May, marking a 40 % year-on-year decline on 2008 levels.  Germany imported nearly 12 percent more cars during the same five-month period.  Exports are unlikely to pick up for at least 18 months until household consumption recovers in key importing economies even including emerging Asia. 

Sales could drop off significantly in 2010 and spur job losses across the industry since the scheme has brought forward potential demand in the market, thereby pre-empting vehicle demand next year. 

In view of this projection, the ruling coalition parties are lobbying for a tax incentive on vehicle purchases when the scheme expires. ## Construction 

Over the past couple of years, construction activity has contracted markedly in numerous developed economies as the financial viability of construction projects has fallen.  A mix of drivers have contributed to the overall contraction in activity.  Assessing residential property first, demand for residential housing has fallen in most developed countries because of an increase in two key areas of uncertainty: (i) the financial position of households; and (ii) the value of housing itself.  Unemployment and the threat of unemployment have played an important adverse role in household decisions to purchase/ move.  Households have been uncertain about the future and those that would like to move/ buy but can afford to wait have chosen to stall their purchasing decision until their outlook becomes more certain. Uncertainty surrounding residential property prices is also leading to a number of households postponing residential property purchases/ moves.  This is especially the case for first time buyers/ households that can afford to wait for some indication of price stabilisation. 

On the supply side, two key drivers have made construction projects less financially viable: higher costs and forced sales.  Cost escalation in the construction industry has been similar to that of many other industries through the boom years but more recently, tighter and more expensive lending conditions have raised project financing costs significantly. Both have contributed to the non-viability of projects, contributing to the slowdown/ contraction in properties coming onto the market.  Forced sales are the other key supply side driver.  As unemployment increases through a recession, some households are forced to sell their properties.  Where price growth had been slowing, this accelerates that slowdown. Where prices were falling, this acts to accelerate the price fall.  Forced selling has led to significant price falls in a number of developed markets, including a number of European markets such as Spain, the UK, Ireland and Denmark. 

Turning to commercial property, the pace of expansion in commercial property exceeded demand in a number of developed economies before the recession took hold in 2008.  With overall economic output contracting rapidly through H2 2008 and into 2009, excess supply of commercial property has increased markedly over the past year.  With excess capacity already built before the recession took hold, the contraction in demand associated with the recession has only exacerbated an already weak market. 

While some of the recent drivers of the developed and developing construction markets are common – high cost of finance and lacking availability of credit being examples, the construction market in developing economies is quite different from that of their developed economy counterparts.  Notably, despite the re

The credit crisis and broader recession has adversely affected construction in Brazil but the worst is likely to have passed. The outlook for Brazil’s construction sector now looks positive with the introduction of major government led construction programmes designed to restart activity in the sector (which accounts for approximately 5% of Brazilian GDP). The government would like the program to be fully underway within the next 6- 12 months but it is worth noting possible delays as developers proceed with caution. Regionally, the program is expected to build 350,000 homes in the North East, 400,000 homes in the South East (including Rio and Sao Paulo), around 100,000 homes in the South and the remaining 150,000 homes in the North and Central Western regions. Brazil is estimated to require 14 million homes for its population of 190 million. To make up the short-fall, this translates to a requirement of approximately 1.2 million new units a year. The Minha Casa Minha Vida program helps to fill the gap and supports poorer households into housing. In addition, the government are considering extending current tax breaks on building materials which are due to expire in the final quarter of this year. In summary, Brazil’s construction sector has suffered from the credit crisis and the global recession. However, the contraction in construction activity appears to have stabilised and with large government led programmes – which look set to be rolled out over the next year, the outlook in the short-term looks positive.
